newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top German opposition figure sticks to euro stance.
newsitem.headline: Top German opposition figure sticks to euro stance.

text.p: Gerhard Schroeder, a leading figure in Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), stood by his cautious view of Europe's planned single currency on Wednesday, despite criticism of his stance.

"When the question of the euro is discussed, the result must not be laid down from the beginning," Schroeder, the premier of Lower Saxony state, told reporters at a meeting of the Bavarian SPD in the southern town of Kloster Irsee.
"When nine currencies come together -- three weak ones, three average ones and three strong ones -- people know that the currency which results will not be the strongest," he said.

Schroeder, who is often mentioned as a likely SPD candidate to challenge Helmut Kohl for the chancellorship in 1998, faced a storm of criticism from government politicians last month after declaring the euro was bound to be weaker than the mark.

After suffering losses in state elections last March for their earlier flirtation with Euro-scepticism, the SPD has reversed its position on the euro in recent months and has said the single currency was the best response to a dominant dollar.
But Schroeder said the SPD should only decide on the introduction of the euro when a number of issues were clearer -- such as who else would be joining the currency union, scheduled to begin in 1999.

He also said any relaxation of the Maastricht criteria countries must meet to enter the currency union would be a major political error, while a delay in the timetable "would not represent an apocalypse".
